extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, dramatists, literary critics, and students of dramatic literature
extracted.subtask_description: Critical guidance and evaluative principles for drama and theatrical writing, focusing on character-consistency, dramatic probability, use of the supernatural, moral effect, language, and stagecraft. Drawn from a literary-critical essay assessing specific plays and scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of the mind as dramatic desideratum
rubrics_metrics.description: Of all power, that of the mind is, on every account, the grand desideratum of human ambition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intellectual power (especially when shown in tension with conscience or a superior will) is a chief source of dramatic interest; the coexistence of great intellectual lordship with guilt excites strong interest because it allows contemplation of intellect as a separate self-subsistence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual superiority plus guilt excites interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The coexistence of great intellectual lordship with guilt has never been adequately represented without exciting the strongest interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters who combine commanding intellect with moral corruption (e.g., Shakespeare’s Richard, Iago, Edmund) are inherently compelling; dramatists should exploit that contrast to sustain audience engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superiority to fear of the invisible world as sublime trait
rubrics_metrics.description: Of all intellectual power, that of superiority to the fear of the invisible world is the most dazzling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A character’s cool intrepidity before ghosts or supernatural threats (example: Don John) can produce sublimity; such superiority can bribe audiences into temporary suspension of judgment and increase dramatic fascination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic probability and harmony of the whole
rubrics_metrics.description: On this propensity ... a specific dramatic probability may be raised by a true poet, if the whole of his work be in harmony: a dramatic probability, sufficient for dramatic pleasure, even when the component characters and incidents border on impossibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poet need only ask the audience to yield themselves to a dream, not to believe literally; provided the whole work is internally harmonious, improbable incidents can be acceptable and pleasurable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet solicits suspension of disbelief, not literal belief
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet does not require us to be awake and believe; he solicits us only to yield ourselves to a dream ... and meantime, only, not to disbelieve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Playwrights may employ the fantastic if they preserve an internal logic and invite an imaginative, not credulous, response from the audience; the audience’s judgment remains 'ready to awaken' at any sign of incongruity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supernatural effects require grounding
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere supernatural effect, without even a hint of any supernatural agency; a prodigy, without any circumstance mentioned that is prodigious; and a miracle introduced without a ground, and ending without a result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introducing storms, miracles, or prodigies without causal hints or consequences is a defect — supernatural events on stage must have plausible grounds or be embedded in the work’s causal fabric, otherwise they read as gratuitous scene-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency and intelligibility of character action
rubrics_metrics.description: The Prior scolds with strained voice ... Yet the author preserves the unity of character, and the scolding Prior from first to last does nothing but scold, with the exception indeed of the last scene ... in which ... he whines, weeps, and kneels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters should act and change in ways intelligible to the audience; abrupt, unexplained reversals (e.g., a lifelong scolder suddenly prostrating himself without motive) violate character unity and weaken dramatic credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Believability of character responses to situations
rubrics_metrics.description: No attempt on the Prior’s part either to prevent him, or to put the mistress and servants of the Castle on their guard against their new inmates ... though he knew ... that Bertram’s 'fearful mates' were assassins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a character is shown to have knowledge or motive, their on-stage behavior should reflect appropriate, believable responses (e.g., prudent action when danger is known); failure to do so is a dramatic fault.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixture of ingredients in right proportion
rubrics_metrics.description: The ingredients too are mixed in the happiest proportion, so as to uphold and relieve each other--more especially in that constant interpoise of wit, gaiety, and social generosity, which prevents the criminal ... from sinking into the mere ruffian.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful characterization often depends on balancing traits (wit, gaiety, generosity) so harsher elements are humanized rather than reduced to stereotypes; proportionate mixture preserves audience sympathy and complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral function: expose hollowness of showy virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: The Atheista Fulminato ... presents an exquisite portraiture of the same qualities, in all their gloss and glow, but presents them for the sole purpose of displaying their hollowness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When plays display 'gentlemanly courage' and honour as mere instruments, they should make their hollowness evident so the audience is warned against mistaking showy accomplishments for true virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: rewarding criminals with sympathy
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole secret of the modern jacobinical drama ... consists in the confusion and subversion of the natural order of things in their causes and effects ... and by rewarding with all the sympathies which are the due of virtue, those criminals ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of dramatic trends that invert moral causation and elicit sympathy for criminality by falsely attributing virtuous qualities to criminals; such confusion can be morally and aesthetically pernicious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retrospective narration should be handled well
rubrics_metrics.description: It tells well and passionately the preliminary circumstances, and thus overcomes the main difficulty of most first acts, to wit, that of retrospective narration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective first acts need to convey past events without clumsy exposition; telling preliminary circumstances passionately and succinctly can solve the retrospective-narration problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'scene for scene' spectacle without purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The first act would have indeed lost its greatest and most sonorous picture; a scene for the sake of a scene, without a word spoken; as such, therefore, (a rarity without a precedent), we must take it, and be thankful!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spectacular scenes that exist purely for show risk being superfluous; they may sometimes be innocent or delightful, but dramatists should ensure spectacle serves narrative, theme, or character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language, metre, and diction must be careful
rubrics_metrics.description: Though crowded with solecisms, corrupt diction, and offences against metre, would possess merits sufficient to out-weigh them, if we could suspend the moral sense during the perusal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faults of diction and metre are real defects; while other strengths can compensate, playwrights should attend to correct, appropriate language and metre rather than rely on performers or audience leniency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depiction of madness should be coherent, not theatrical gimmick
rubrics_metrics.description: Which in theatrical language is called the madness, but which the author more accurately entitles, delirium, it appearing indeed a sort of intermittent fever with fits of lightheadedness off and on, whenever occasion and stage effect happen to call for it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Madness on stage should grow from character and circumstance; intermittent, opportunistic 'fits' used merely for effect are theatrically cheap and undermine plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid inconsistent or plagiarised imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: These two lines consist in a senseless plagiarism from the counterfeited madness of Edgar in Lear ... and the no less senseless adoption of Dryden’s forest fiend ... Observe too these images stand unique in the speeches of Imogine, without the slightest resemblance to anything she says before or after.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Borrowed images or lines that do not fit the speaker’s established voice or the play’s diction appear incongruous; originality and voice-consistency are crucial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage spectacle should not replace cause-and-effect intelligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Every event and every scene of the play might have taken place as well if Bertram and his vessel had been driven in by a common hard gale ... a prodigy, without any circumstance mentioned that is prodigious; and a miracle introduced without a ground, and ending without a result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audiences require a sense of causal relation; storms, wrecks, and other stage spectacles must be integrated into the causal narrative to avoid feeling arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid gratuitous indecency and pandering to gross stimulants
rubrics_metrics.description: I want words to describe the mingled horror and disgust with which I witnessed the opening of the fourth act, considering it as a melancholy proof of the depravation of the public mind ... craving alone for the grossest and most outrageous stimulants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appealing to baser appetites (gratuitous sexual or violent spectacle) can be a sign of moral and aesthetic degradation; playwrights should consider moral effects and not pander to gross tastes for applause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious with religious representation on stage
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the fifth act, the only thing noticeable ... is the profane representation of the high altar in a chapel, with all the vessels and other preparations for the holy sacrament. A hymn is actually sung on the stage by the chorister boys!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portrayal of sacred rites on stage risks profanation and audience offense; dramatists should handle religious material with sensitivity and purpose, not mere stage novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide coherent resolution and intelligible consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: It sometimes happens that we are punished for our faults by incidents, in the causation of which these faults had no share ... The sense of Before and After becomes both intelligible and intellectual when, and only when, we contemplate the succession in the relations of Cause and Effect ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramas should show appropriate consequences for actions and maintain intelligible causal chains; lack of proportional relation between antecedents and consequents causes discomfort and undermines moral intelligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of character-contrasts to reveal moral truth
rubrics_metrics.description: This, indeed, is the moral value of the play at large, and that which places it at a world’s distance from the spirit of modern jacobinism ... presents them for the sole purpose of displaying their hollowness, and in order to put us on our guard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasting showy accomplishments with true virtue can be a deliberate moral strategy: present 'virtues' in contexts that reveal their hollowness, so the audience recognizes the distinction between appearance and moral worth.
